notes.heading: Cations, anions and ion formation
points: Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive cations; non-metal atoms gain electrons to form negative anions.
A cation has more protons than electrons; an anion has more electrons than protons. Neutrons carry no charge.
Na (1s2 2s2 2p6 3s1) loses one electron to give Na+ (1s2 2s2 2p6), which has the same configuration as neon.
Group 1, 2, 13 form 1+, 2+, 3+; groups 15, 16, 17 form 3–, 2–, 1–; noble gases form no ions.
Losing electrons is oxidation, gaining is reduction, so making an ionic compound from its elements is a redox reaction.

notes.heading: Transition element ions with variable charge
points: A transition element has a partially filled d sublevel and can form ions of more than one charge, e.g. Fe2+ and Fe3+.
In first-row transition elements, 4s electrons are lost before 3d electrons when ions form.
Most form 2+ ions by losing the two 4s electrons, e.g. Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6.
Variable charges occur because 4s and 3d are close in energy, shown by successive ionization energy data.

notes.heading: Ionic bonding, formulas and naming
points: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Naming: cation first, then anion; a monatomic anion keeps the start of its parent name and ends in -ide.
Polyatomic ions to learn: NH4+, OH–, NO3–, HCO3–, CO3 2–, SO4 2–, PO4 3–.
To find a formula, balance ion numbers so net charge is zero (bar diagrams or criss-cross), then simplify the ratio.
Bracket a polyatomic ion when more than one is needed, e.g. Al(NO3)3, Ca3N2, Na2CO3.

notes.heading: Ionic lattices and lattice enthalpy
points: Ionic compounds are continuous 3D lattices of repeating cations and anions; the formula is an empirical formula giving the ion ratio.
Ionic bonding is non-directional: each ion attracts all oppositely charged neighbours equally.
Lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy change to turn one mole of solid lattice into gaseous ions; it is endothermic, e.g. MX(s) → M+(g) + X–(g).
Larger lattice enthalpy means stronger ionic bonding, and it rises with higher ionic charge and falls with larger ionic radius.
Example: NaF (930 kJ mol–1) exceeds KF (829) due to smaller cation; CaF2 (2651) is mainly high because of the 2+ charge.

notes.heading: Properties of ionic compounds
points: High melting and boiling points and low volatility, because strong electrostatic attractions must be overcome.
Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, as ions are fixed; molten or aqueous ones conduct because ions are mobile.
Usually soluble in polar solvents like water, where partial charges on water molecules pull ions out of the lattice.
Insoluble in non-polar solvents such as hexane, since there is no attraction between ions and solvent.
Insoluble if lattice attraction is stronger than ion–water attraction, e.g. calcium carbonate and silver chloride.

definitions.definition: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons, so it has more protons than electrons.
definitions.trap: Saying cations gain protons; the number of protons never changes, only electrons.

definitions.definition: A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons, so it has more electrons than protons.
definitions.trap: Mixing up cation and anion, or forgetting anions get the -ide ending.

definitions.definition: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (cations and anions).
definitions.trap: Defining it as electron transfer; the bond is the attraction, not the transfer.

definitions.definition: An ion made up of several atoms bonded together that carries an overall charge, such as NH4+ or SO4 2–.
definitions.trap: Splitting the ion up or changing its formula when writing compounds.

definitions.definition: Describes different species that have the same electron configuration.
definitions.trap: Saying they have the same number of protons; only the electrons match.

definitions.definition: An element with a partially filled d sublevel, which can form ions of different charges.
definitions.trap: Calling zinc a transition element; it only forms 2+ ions.

definitions.definition: A measure of the ability of an atom to attract a pair of covalently bonded electrons.
definitions.trap: Omitting that it refers to atoms in a bond.

definitions.definition: The standard enthalpy change when one mole of a solid ionic lattice forms gaseous ions; endothermic.
definitions.trap: Writing the reverse process (gaseous ions to lattice) or giving a negative value.

definitions.definition: A continuous three-dimensional network of repeating positive and negative ions held by electrostatic attractions.
definitions.trap: Describing ionic compounds as separate molecules.

definitions.definition: The simplest whole-number ratio of each type of ion in the lattice.
definitions.trap: Treating the formula as a molecule, e.g. CaF2 molecules.

definitions.definition: The tendency of a substance to vaporize, turning into a gas.
definitions.trap: Saying ionic compounds are volatile; they are non-volatile.
